# 1 Kings 20:1–22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Passage

**Matthew Henry** observes that this chapter is the history of a war between Ben-hadad king of Syria and Ahab king of Israel in which Ahab was twice victorious. Henry notes that Elijah and Elisha are absent from this story — Jezebel's rage had cooled, and Elijah was busy founding prophetic schools. God favoured the nation with these successes so that "if possible, they might be led to repentance by the goodness of God."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Ellicott** notes that this chapter is "evidently drawn from a different source" than the Elijah narratives, belongs to the latter years of Ahab's reign, and shows it was a time of "no inconsiderable prosperity." The presence of prophetic schools suggests that Jezebel's influence for Baal had been "reduced to impotence."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

**Dale Ralph Davis** (quoted in Precept Austin) summarizes chs. 20–22 as a triad "in which each chapter emphasizes the failure of Ahab and how the word of God stands opposed to him."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary

---

## v. 1 — Ben-hadad's Siege of Samaria

**Traditional Reading:** Ben-hadad ("son of Hadad," a dynastic title like Pharaoh) assembled his entire force — including thirty-two vassal kings from the region — with horses and chariots, and besieged Samaria. The 32 kings were "petty princes, such as were in the land of Canaan in Joshua's time" (Gill) or "heads of families" and "governors of cities under Benhadad." The campaign's motive is not stated explicitly, but Gill suggests either ambition or Ahab's refusal to pay tribute previously imposed by Ben-hadad's father. God's providential purpose was to use this as "a scourge to Ahab for his impiety."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-1.htm (Gill, Benson, Cambridge, Pulpit)

**Pulpit Commentary** adds: "The object of this expedition was clearly to humble and to plunder the kingdom of Samaria… Ben-hadad was clearly a vain and overbearing and tyrannical prince, and the only crime of Israel may have been that it was independent of him, or had refused to do him homage."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-1.htm

**Precept Austin** notes Samaria's strategic natural defences: located about 30 miles north of Jerusalem, with three steep slopes making assaults difficult and its own water supply. Besieging rather than storming was the attackers' only option.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary

---

## vv. 2–3 — Ben-hadad's First Demand

**Traditional Reading:** Ben-hadad sent messengers into the besieged city demanding Ahab's silver, gold, and "best wives and children." **Ellicott** interprets this as "the assertion and acceptance of Syrian sovereignty over Israel: all the possessions and the family of the vassal are acknowledged to be the property of his superior lord."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

**Matthew Henry** sees this as designed to gall: "'All shall be mine, without exception.'"
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Pulpit Commentary** remarks that the mention of Ahab's wives is especially telling — "the surrender of the harem is a virtual surrender of the throne… and certainly a surrender of all manhood and self-respect." Ben-hadad's aim was "to wound Ahab in his tenderest point, to humble him to the lowest depths of degradation, and possibly to force a quarrel upon him."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary

**Precept Austin** calls it a "humiliating request."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary

---

## v. 4 — Ahab's Surrender

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab capitulated completely: "My lord, O king… I am yours, along with all that I have." This was an unconditional surrender.

**Matthew Henry** provides the classic moral reading: "See the effect of sin. (1.) If he had not by sin provoked God to depart from him, Ben-hadad could not have made such a demand. Sin brings men into such straits, by putting them out of divine protection. If God may not rule us, our enemies shall. A rebel to God is a slave to all besides. … (2.) If he had not by sin wronged his own conscience, and set that against him, he could not have made such a mean surrender. Guilt dispirits men, and makes them cowards."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word (Guzik)** adds: "Ahab's response to Ben-Hadad fit his general personality. He was a man concerned with the luxuries and comforts of living, and so he did not have the character to stand in the face of such a threat." Guzik also notes that "the national and military might of Israel was greatly weakened by the three-and-a-half-year drought and famine that had just ended."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Precept Austin** calls Ahab "spineless… willing to compromise family and wealth in face of the military threat," and cites Leviticus 26:36 — "I will also bring weakness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary

---

## vv. 5–6 — Ben-hadad's Escalated Demand

**Traditional Reading:** The messengers returned with an even more aggressive demand: Ben-hadad would send his servants the next day to search and strip Ahab's palace and the houses of his officials, taking "all that is precious to you."

**Ellicott** calls this "virtually for the plunder of Samaria" and suggests it "probably neither expects nor desires acceptance, and is therefore a refusal of all but unconditional surrender. It is notable that in the last extremity Ahab falls back on an exceptional appeal to the patriotism of the people."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

**Matthew Henry** notes Ben-hadad's greed: "He thinks it not enough to call it his, unless he have it in his hands." Henry describes him as "as covetous as he is proud… as spiteful as he is haughty… as unreasonable as he is unjust."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** cites Patterson and Austel: "When Ahab agreed to his terms readily, Ben-Hadad demanded the additional right to unlimited search of the palace and the houses of Ahab's officials so as to carry away anything of value."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

---

## vv. 7–8 — Ahab Consults the Elders

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab summoned the elders of the land, acknowledged the situation ("this man is looking for trouble"), and noted he had not refused the initial demand. The elders and people unanimously advised resistance: "Do not listen to him or consent to his terms."

**Enduring Word (Guzik)** observes: "It was wiser for Ahab to seek the counsel of the elders of the land before he surrendered… The elders of Israel rightly saw that such surrender to Ben-Hadad and the Syrians was the first step to a total loss of sovereignty for Israel. If they wanted to remain a kingdom at all, they had to resist this threat."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Matthew Henry** characterises Ahab's speech as "poorly" done — he "appeals to them whether Ben-hadad be not an unreasonable enemy" — yet the elders "speak bravely," promising "no doubt to stand by him in the refusal."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

---

## v. 9 — Ahab's Qualified Refusal

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab replied that he would fulfil the first demand but "this thing I cannot do." 

**Matthew Henry** notes Ahab "expresses himself very modestly in his denial… He owns Ben-hadad's dominion over him… but this thing I may not do; I must not give what is none of my own." Henry adds: "It was a mortification to Ben-hadad that even such an abject spirit as Ahab's durst deny him; yet it should seem, by his manner of expressing himself, that he durst not have done it if his people had not animated him."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** notes the practical reality: "to deny a tyrant on one point is to deny him on every point. Ahab could expect a harsh reaction."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

---

## v. 10 — Ben-hadad's Oath of Destruction

**Traditional Reading:** Ben-hadad swore by his gods that Samaria would be so utterly destroyed that not enough dust would remain to give each of his soldiers a handful.

**Pulpit Commentary** explains: "The phrase probably implies a threat of destruction, as well as a boast of overwhelming strength."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-10.htm

**Matthew Henry:** "In his fury, he imprecates the impotent revenge of his gods, if the dust of Samaria serve for handfuls for his army… so numerous, so resolute, an army… Thus confident is his pride, thus cruel is his malice; this prepares him to be ruined."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** notes that Jezebel swore a similar oath against Elijah (1 Kings 19:2), suggesting a cultural formula for solemn curses.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

---

## v. 11 — Ahab's Proverbial Reply

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab answered: "The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off." 

**Matthew Henry** calls this "one of the wisest words that ever Ahab spoke, and is a good item or momento to us all; it is folly to boast beforehand of any day, since we know not what it may bring forth (Prov. 27:1), but especially to boast of a day of battle… Apply it to our spiritual conflicts. Peter fell by his confidence. While we are here we are but girding on the harness, and therefore must never boast as though we had put it off. Happy is the man that feareth always, and is never off his watch."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** echoes this: "The idea is that you should do your boasting after the battle, not before."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

---

## v. 12 — Ben-hadad Orders Attack While Drinking

**Traditional Reading:** Ben-hadad received Ahab's message while drinking with the allied kings in their "tents" (or "pavilions" — KJV; literally "booths" or temporary shelters) and ordered his forces into position against the city.

**Matthew Henry** highlights the moral peril: "Drunkenness is a sin which armies and their officers have of old been addicted to… Had he not been very secure he would not have sat to drink; and, had he not been intoxicated, he would not have been so very secure. Security and sensuality went together in the old world, and Sodom… Ben-hadad's drunkenness was the forerunner of his fall, as Belshazzar's was."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

---

## v. 13 — The Unnamed Prophet Promises Victory

**Traditional Reading:** An unnamed prophet approached Ahab with the word of the LORD: "Do you see this entire great army? Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD."

**Matthew Henry** expresses wonder "that God should send a prophet with a kind and gracious message to so wicked a prince as Ahab." He gives three reasons: (1) for Israel's sake as "the seed of Abraham his friend and Jacob his chosen"; (2) to magnify His mercy toward "one so evil and unthankful"; (3) "to mortify the pride of Ben-hadad and check his insolence." Henry adds: "Ahab, in his prosperity, would not have borne the sight of him, but now he bids him welcome, when none of the prophets of the groves can give him any assistance. He enquired not for a prophet of the Lord, but God sent one to him unasked, for he waits to be gracious."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Ellicott** notes that this unnamed prophet's appearance shows "Ahab's enmity to the prophetic order was over since the great day at Carmel, and that the schools of the prophets were forming themselves again." He adds that Elijah does not appear in these political functions, "reserving himself for the higher moral and religious mission from God."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** suggests the prophet "does not seem to be either Elijah or Elisha. He was one of the 7,000 in Israel that were quietly faithful to Yahweh." Guzik also notes the irony: "Ahab saw the victory of Yahweh over the pagan god Baal on Mount Carmel – yet he was not completely convinced. Graciously, God would give him even more evidence."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Gill** (summarised on StudyLight) says Jewish writers supposed this prophet to be Micaiah the son of Imlah (1 Kings 22:9), "one of those perhaps that Obadiah hid in the cave."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-20.html

---

## v. 14 — By Whom? The Young Officers

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab asked "By whom?" and the prophet answered: "By the young officers of the district governors." Ahab asked who would start the battle, and the prophet said, "You will."

**Matthew Henry** explains the divine strategy: the young men were "only 232, utterly unacquainted with war, and the unlikeliest men that could be thought of for such a bold attempt; yet these must do it, these weak and foolish things must be instruments of confounding the wise and strong, that, while Ben-hadad's boasting is punished, Ahab's may be prevented and precluded, and the excellency of the power may appear to be of God."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** applies this pastorally: "Whenever a work for God is to be done, we often ask Ahab's question: 'By whom?'… God's normal way of working is to use the people already with the Christian leader, even if they seem to be a very unlikely army."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Ellicott** identifies the young men as "the attendants or armour-bearers of the territorial chiefs, no doubt picked men and well armed."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

---

## v. 15 — The Muster: 232 Young Officers and 7,000 Troops

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab mustered 232 young officers of the district governors, followed by the rest of the Israelite army — 7,000 in all.

**Matthew Henry** finds it "observable that it is the same number with theirs that had not bowed the knee to Baal (ch. 19:18), though, it is likely, not the same men."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** similarly notes: "Undoubtedly, these were not the same seven thousand that stayed faithful to God in Israel, but there was a correspondence between their numbers to show that God could and would work through each group."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Ellicott** assesses: "The whole garrison is stated as seven thousand — enough, perhaps, to man the walls, but wholly unfit to take the field."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

---

## v. 16 — The Noon Sortie; Ben-hadad Getting Drunk

**Traditional Reading:** The Israelites marched out at noon while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings were in their tents getting drunk.

**Enduring Word:** "The same sinful heart that made Ben-Hadad attack Israel also made him a drunk. In part, his own weak character defeated him."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Matthew Henry** notes the time of day — noon — was when the enemy was resting and drinking; Ben-hadad was "drinking himself drunk… Security and sensuality went together."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Ellicott** adds (citing Josephus) that the sally was made "at noon, when the besiegers were resting unarmed in the heat of the day."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

---

## vv. 17–18 — Ben-hadad's Foolish Order

**Traditional Reading:** The young officers marched out first. Scouts reported "men marching out of Samaria." Ben-hadad ordered: whether they come for peace or war, "take them alive."

**Matthew Henry** judges this order as "imprudent": Ben-hadad was "far gone" in drink and gave orders "not to kill them, which might have been done more easily and safely, but to seize them, which gave them an opportunity of killing the aggressors; so imprudent was he in the orders he gave, as well as unjust, in ordering them to be taken prisoners though they came for peace."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** suggests alternatively: "It may be that Ben-Hadad intended to say that if the men from Israel had come for war, they should be attacked and killed. Perhaps he spoke in a drunken confusion, giving foolish orders to his soldiers."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

---

## vv. 19–20 — The Battle: Each Struck Down His Opponent

**Traditional Reading:** The young officers marched out, the army behind them, and each struck down his opponent. The Arameans fled with Israel in pursuit. Ben-hadad escaped on horseback with the cavalry.

**Gill** explains: "The Syrian army, or at least a body of men detached from them, met them, opposed them, and fought them, and they slew of them 7232 men; as many as they themselves were." The Targum says Ben-hadad escaped "with two couple of horsemen."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-20.html

**Ellicott** compares this victory to Jonathan's slaughter of the Philistine garrison (1 Samuel 14) and Gideon's rout of Midian (Judges 7), adding: "It does not necessarily follow that the event was miraculous. Such dispersions of vast Oriental armies are not uncommon in history. The lesson is that drawn with noble simplicity by Jonathan: 'There is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few' (1 Samuel 14:6)."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

**Enduring Word** cites Patterson and Austel on the battle strategy: "to send out the small but well trained advance party who could perhaps draw near to the Syrians without arousing too much alarm and then, at a given signal, initiate a charge that, joined by Ahab's main striking force, would both catch the drunken Arameans off guard and throw them into confusion. The plan was more successful than Ahab dared to imagine."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

---

## v. 21 — Ahab's Pursuit: Great Slaughter

**Traditional Reading:** The king of Israel marched out and attacked the horses and chariots, inflicting a great slaughter on the Arameans.

**Gill** notes Josephus's report that "Ahab had another army within the walls" and that after the victory the Israelites "plundered the camp, in which was much riches, and great plenty of gold and silver, and took their chariots and horses, and returned to the city of Samaria."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-20.html

**Matthew Henry** reflects: "God oftentimes makes one wicked man a scourge to another."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

---

## v. 22 — The Prophet Advises Preparation for Spring

**Traditional Reading:** The prophet told Ahab: "Go and strengthen your position, and take note what you must do, for in the spring the king of Aram will come up against you."

**Matthew Henry** observes: "It should seem, he was now secure, and looked but a little way before him. Those that are careless of their souls are often as careless of their outward affairs." The prophet's advice shows that "God had decreed the end, but Ahab must use the means, else he tempts God: 'Help thyself, strengthen thyself, and God will help and strengthen thee.'"
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

**Gill** paraphrases: the prophet "exhorted him to fortify his cities, especially Samaria, and increase his army, that he might be able to oppose the king of Syria," and also to "observe his moral and religious actions, and take heed that he did not offend the Lord by them, as well as make military preparations."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-20.html

**Enduring Word** notes: "The prophet knew that God works through the careful preparation of His people." The victory did not end the conflict; Ben-hadad would return.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

**Precept Austin** adds that the prophet gives Ahab four commands — essentially, prepare for a second attack: "While God would bring about the victory, He was telling Ahab that Israel had a responsibility to do their part (God's sovereignty and Man's responsibility is the pattern throughout the Bible)."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary

---

## Protestant Traditions: Points of Distinctive Emphasis

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The Reformed reading (evident in **Matthew Henry** and **Dale Ralph Davis**) stresses God's sovereignty even over pagan kings, the interplay of divine decree and human means (v. 22), and the principle that God grants victories to wicked kings for His own name's sake, not theirs. Davis sees chs. 20–22 as a unified literary-theological triad displaying "Ahab's repeated (and fatal) opposition to the word of Yahweh."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-20-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_kings/20.htm

### Baptist
**Gill (Reformed Baptist)** focuses on historical detail: identifying the Ben-hadad as "Benhadad the second," noting the 32 kings were "petty princes, such as were in the land of Canaan in Joshua's time," and emphasising God's providence in using the attack "as a scourge to Ahab for his impiety." Gill also notes the Jewish tradition identifying the unnamed prophet as Micaiah.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-20.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word)
**David Guzik** emphasises God working through "unlikely instruments," applying v. 14 to Christian leadership: "God's normal way of working is to use the people already with the Christian leader, even if they seem to be a very unlikely army." He highlights the Spirit's miraculous working and the theme that God gives repeated evidence of His power — even to stubborn Ahab.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-20/

### Anglican (Ellicott, Cambridge)
**Ellicott** takes a more historically measured approach, noting the chapter "does not necessarily follow that the event was miraculous" and comparing the victory to other ancient routs of large Oriental armies. He emphasises the chapter as evidence of restored prophetic activity after Carmel and Ahab's "return in profession to the allegiance to Jehovah."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/20.htm

### Methodist (Benson, Wesleyan tradition)
**Benson** sees God's design in the war as punishment "for their apostacy and idolatry" and identifies the 32 kings as "either subject or tributary to Ben-hadad, or hired by him."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/20-1.htm

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **God's mercy to the undeserving:** Even wicked Ahab received divine aid — for Israel's sake, to humble Ben-hadad's pride, and to vindicate God's own name.
2. **The folly of pride:** Ben-hadad's drunken boasting is a textbook case of Proverbs 16:18 — pride before destruction.
3. **God uses weak instruments:** The 232 young officers and 7,000 troops prefigure the biblical pattern that God saves "by many or by few."
4. **Sovereignty and responsibility:** God decreed victory but required Ahab to prepare and fight — a balance all traditions affirm.
5. **The proverb of v. 11:** Universally cited as timeless wisdom — do not boast before the battle is won; applied spiritually to the believer's lifelong warfare against sin.
